purpose: Assesses whether the organization can detect or prevent an adversary from using knowledge of and access to a target AI system to tailor an attack before it's launched.
summary: AI Attack Staging consists of techniques adversaries use to prepare an attack on the target model, including training proxy models, poisoning the target model, and crafting adversarial data. Some of these techniques can be performed entirely offline, making them difficult to detect or mitigate before the attack is deployed.
expectedStatementElements: How the organization would detect an adversary training a proxy model against exposed inference APIs or public artifacts
What controls limit an adversary's ability to verify an adversarial attack works before deploying it
How adversarial-example robustness is tested and monitored for production models
What logging exists for API query patterns that resemble model replication or extraction attempts
evidenceExamples: Inference API query logs showing volume/pattern analysis for extraction-style behavior
Adversarial robustness testing results or red-team reports
Documentation of any offline model-hardening or adversarial training performed
Records of public artifact exposure (datasets, pretrained weights) reviewed for staging risk
commonGaps: No monitoring exists for query patterns consistent with model replication (e.g., high-volume systematic querying)
Adversarial robustness has never been tested against the production model
Publicly available artifacts (sample data, model cards) give more staging detail than necessary
interviewQuestions: Could someone build a working copy of our model just by querying our API? How would we know if they tried?
Have we ever tested our model against adversarial examples designed to fool it?
What public information exists about our model architecture or training data that an attacker could use to tailor an attack?
If an attacker verified their attack offline, would we see any trace of that before it's used against us?
